Despite significant progress, the GM task poses a challenge due to its difficulty in generalizing across disparate graph types. This limitation is addressed in our proposed framework by treating graph data as embedded vectors and applying self-supervised learning to enhance their representational integrity. Our framework, entitled Self-Expressive Graph Matching (SEGM), aims to learn unique vector representations for pairs of graphs while maintaining their structural uniqueness. In practice, SEGM achieves this by pairing graphs for self-supervised training with an encoder and decoder, with an added uniqueness constraint to ensure that matched graph pairs have unique, invariant representations. Our empirical evaluations, conducted across nine public datasets, reveal that SEGM outperforms leading GM baselines in multiple assessment metrics. characterizing indoor environments through 3D mapping has become a significant area of study.  Reconstructing a 3D environment from 2D images is a complex task, primarily because it necessitates substantial data sets.  Estimating the camera's position and orientation from a single image, also known as scene understanding, can streamline this process by reducing the need for 3D reconstruction.  Utilizing a single image allows for the direct incorporation of visual data, making it a robust method for mapping indoor environments.  This paper presents an indoor localization system called Visual Indoor Explorer (VIE),  which utilizes a single image to estimate the camera's position and orientation within a pre-mapped environment,  or create a 3D map from a set of images.  VIE's core functionality is built around the PM3 method for 3D reconstruction and re-projection error for orientation calibration,  which the system uses to calculate the camera's position and orientation.  This method is complemented by the PM3 method for re-construction and re-projection error for orientation calibration,  which the system uses to calculate the camera's position and orientation within a pre-mapped environment.  Experimental results show that VIE's indoor localization system outperforms existing methods using re-construction and re-projection error for orientation calibration,  specifically the VisualVO method,  which utilizes re-construction and re-projection error for orientation calibration and poses calculated from 2D-3D correspondences,  by achieving an average accuracy rate of 1.15m and 0.45m in localizing poses within a pre-mapped environment and creating 3D maps from a set of images respectively.  Furthermore,  VIE demonstrates re-localization capability in novel views and against background,  as well as robust performance in the presence of occlusions and dynamic environments.  This is illustrated through pose accuracy rates of 0.69m and 0.53m for re-localization in a pre-mapped environment and against a background respectively.  Additionally,  VIE's re-construction and re-projection error for orientation calibration,  specifically the VisualVO method,  is evaluated for indoor localization and re-localization in a pre-mapped environment against a background,  which shows robust performance in the presence of occlusions and dynamic environments.  This is illustrated through pose accuracy rates of 0.69m and 0.53m for re-localization in a pre-mapped environment and against a background respectively.

chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), but existing technology has 
limited portability and accuracy. A novel approach to COPD management is 
proposed, leveraging IOT-based wireless respiratory monitoring with improved 
accuracy. A key component of this system is a machine learning algorithm 
developed using neural networks to enhance data quality, but it requires large 
datasets for training. Although public COPD datasets are minimal, a new 
database of 1000 annotated audio recordings from COPD patients has been created 
and made available for researchers. This database consists of 5000-minute 
recordings from 50 different speakers, featuring various speaking tasks that 
indicate different breathing patterns. Additionally, distinct COPD symptoms such 
as speech, breathing, and cough sounds are classified using a new dataset of 
1000-minute recordings from 20 speakers. Experimental results show that a 
neural-based classification algorithm achieves exceptional performance in detecting 
these symptoms compared to conventional machine learning methods. Furthermore, 
our research presents initial findings on analyzing the acoustic characteristics 
of COPD symptoms, and a proposed framework for developing more precise lung 
monitoring systems using machine learning is outlined. These findings contribute 
substantially to the development of innovative COPD management systems. 

  In this research, our goals are to create, validate, and compare multiple 
machine learning models capable of identifying respiratory symptoms from audio 
recordings. A novel approach to enhancing data quality is introduced by incorporating 
domain knowledge, and our proposed framework for developing more accurate lung 
monitoring systems is disclosed. Additionally, our newly created database of 
respiratory symptoms is made available for researchers to advance COPD management 
technologies. 

  In the field of respiratory research, high-quality datasets are scarce, 
especially those encompassing speaking tasks that incorporate different breathing 
patterns. To bridge this gap, we present a new database of respiratory symptoms 
from audio recordings, known as the RSP-Dataset, which includes various speaking 
tasks that incorporate different breathing patterns and is available for download 
along with our methodology. This dataset consists of 1000-minute recordings from 
20 speakers, who uttered the same sentences while exhibiting distinct respiratory 
symptoms such as coughing and breathing. Moreover, our research involves the 
development of multiple machine learning algorithms capable of identifying these 
respiratory symptoms from audio recordings. 

  In this study, we introduce the RSP-Dataset and present results from testing 
our proposed machine learning algorithms on this dataset.

Our analysis focuses on the mid-plane projections of weakly non-linearly perturbed cosmological models, using the Lagrangian perturbation theory to model density field fluctuations. However, RNN's struggled with scaling RNNs due to their fundamental limitations in design.  Transformer Architectures overcame this challenge by replacing RNNs with self-attention mechanisms that eliminated sequential limitations.  Yet, many models combined the two, arguing that RNNs contributed valuable hierarchical representations.  Our research takes a contrasting view, believing that RNNs' historical effectiveness stemmed from their ability to learn similar sequential patterns present in natural language.  To test this, we developed a related task using medical code analysis, extracting sequential patterns from tree structures.  Our results showed that RNNs' performance could be matched using the self-attention mechanism once the sequential structure was uncovered.  This found support in our ablations and further highlighted that RNNs' ability to extract these patterns was fundamentally linked to their ability to recognize similar patterns present in data.  This was compounded by the incorporation of pre-training, a phenomenon we dubbed the "pattern preservation problem".  This phenomenon has broad implications, could be particularly consequential in large model evaluations, and demands close scrutiny in future research. better overall system performance. This is particularly evident when the system

problems through simple, robust, and easily interpretable solutions.  Ultimately,

initiatives, allowing for the exploration of system-level outcomes in a more realistic

We demonstrate that when the boundary of the area is smooth, a minimal amount of information, related to the Monge-Ampere measure, is sufficient to deduce the Hamilton-Jacobi equation's coefficients across the entire area. In regions with non-flat boundaries, we establish a weaker version of this capability, where we can recover the coefficients near a boundary segment provided that the information is proportional to the Neumann boundary measure. These results are derived through a combination of classical unique continuation techniques and the Hamilton-Jacobi equation's specific characteristics, particularly the appearance of non-negative monotonic functions. Our method's key component is the development of a new monotonic function when the boundary is smooth, or an integrated monotonic function when the boundary is not smooth, which helps to recover the Hamilton-Jacobi equation's coefficients. Additionally, we provide an example related to the Schrödinger equation to show that the available quantitative unique continuation result is optimal. Our research also includes an alternative proof for the classical unique continuation property of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation based on the determinantal Green's function. This alternative proof's component, where we integrate the Green's function with respect to the Monge-Ampere measure, is significant because it may be applied to higher-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi equations and other nonlinear first-order partial differential equations. Lastly, we discuss the challenges and possibilities of modifying our strategy to address other types of Hamilton-Jacobi equations, such as those with unbounded coefficients, multiple variables, and non-compact domains.

By selecting the most informative images to label, we reduce the need for traditional supervised training methods that require extensive labeling.   Abstract:
  We analyzed the temperature and iron column density variations in the spectra
  of nearby M-dwarfs, discovering a positive correlation between stars with dust
  emission and elevated gas temperatures. Utilizing APERO and CARMENES data, we
  obtained temperature and iron column density measurements for 229 M-dwarfs,
  including 103 with dust emission. We compared their temperatures to a reference
  value, finding a significant increase in temperatures above 3000 K, indicating
  a potential future for sensitive spectroscopy in detecting dust around M-dwarfs.
  We propose a new criterion for dust detection based on a M-dwarf's mass,
  yielding a detection rate of about 30%. While most detected dust clouds are
  associated with M-dwarfs in binary systems, certain isolated stars also exhibit
  dust emission. Further analysis suggests that dust emission is more prevalent
  in M-dwarfs with higher angular momentum, possibly indicating a potential
  future for dust detection as an indicator of angular momentum in low-mass
  stars.

This research proposes a 1D sound-like machine learning-based model to simulate the quantum hydrodynamic theory of quasiparticle-starved systems. It demonstrates that a quantum phase transition from the starved phase to normal matter can be precisely controlled using a quasiparticle injection mechanism. Additionally, it shows that the quantum transition can be dominated by a sound-like quasiparticle coexistence region, and that this sound-like behavior can be used to accurately measure the critical exponent and transition temperature. For example, for systems like caloron lattices based on SU(2) GL(3) symmetry, where the normal phase has a temperature as low as 1.1K, the sound-like mode becomes dominant at temperatures just above 0.1K. This process is further complicated in regions with geographic isolation by local government decisions. These authorities typically rely on predictive modeling of the virus's transmission and immunization process to make data-driven decisions. A random effect Proportional To Size (PTS) algorithm for systematic sampling is an accurate method for estimating the virus's spread, gathering immunization data, and allocating samples to different areas for further investigation. This research also highlights the robustness of the PTS algorithm in maintaining coherent and meaningful results even when the sample size is relatively small. These models have been proven to excel in tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and graph classification.  While traditional neural networks leverage input data represented as connected nodes, they fail to capture the inherent structural relationships between the data.  In contrast, graph-based neural network models utilize the structural information inherent in the data, which is critical in many domains, such as physical networks, social networks, and biological networks.  However, the process of converting raw data into structural information, which is fundamental in developing graph-based neural network models, has not been thoroughly explored.  To address this limitation, we will delve into the discipline of unsupervised graph embedding, which aims to convert raw data into structural information by learning a real-valued representation for the graph's nodes.  A comprehensive survey of graph embedding techniques has been conducted, and we have categorized them based on embedding objectives, such as proximity, structure, and label information.  We have also examined notable unsupervised graph embedding algorithms, which have been recognized for their ability to learn meaningful node representations, thereby enhancing the performance of subsequent machine learning tasks.  A discussion on challenges, potential research directions, and applications of graph embedding has been facilitated through influential datasets and benchmarking protocols.  Finally, a related work survey of graph classification, which has been enabled by these embedding techniques, has been presented, along with prominent models and protocols.  To further accelerate future research, the source code of influential embedding algorithms has been made publicly available. motivations and content of late Antiquity's didactic poems, a literary genre that spanned from the 1st to the 5th centuries. We concentrate on the union of two concepts: the theoretical properties of these poems' language and their capacity to convey moral and intellectual knowledge. Our analysis specific to the Greek world reveals that critics have alternately viewed the works of authors such as Oppian, Phildelphos, and Consbruchos as either purely aesthetic pieces or else straightforward vessels of scientific knowledge. In contrast, our research embraces a more complex perspective, combining elements from both approaches. We propose that the form of these didactic poems, characterized by a structured and often rhyming language, not only fosters a sense of anticipation in the reader but also successfully avoids the monotony commonly associated with scientific treatises. In the case of the Latin world, our focus falls on Lucan and Flavius Cresconius Corippus, while also mentioning other lesser-known authors. Our primary objective is to navigate the intricate relationship between these authors' personal biases and their stated goals of educating the reader. We maintain that the most compelling works are those where the writer's character and the narrative's development are equally well-integrated. We further recognize that the evolution of the didactic poem form was inevitably influenced by the historical context in which they were written, albeit in ways that are at times more implicit than explicit. We propose that the best approach to understanding these authors is through a combined critical methodology, incorporating elements from both the ancient critics' philosophies and modern theoretical frameworks. We choose to explore the most pressing questions that arise when reading these authors rather than attempting a comprehensive historical survey of the genre as a whole. Our primary concern is to initiate a fresh conversation regarding the didactic poems of Late Antiquity rather than to provide a definitive summary of the existing research. This is because tests typically aim to evaluate the computation's output given its input, but many computational models produce multiple outputs based on how the behaviors are combined. This issue stems from the unclear nature of combined outputs, which can result from various combinations of the model's underlying behaviors. This problem is exacerbated in computational models that incorporate non-deterministic and probabilistic elements, making it difficult to parse their combined outputs. To address this difficulty, we propose a new approach to testing these types of computational models. This approach focuses only on the computation's output for specific, particular inputs, disregarding issues with the model's underlying behaviors. In effect, this approach reduces testing these computational models to the same problem as testing deterministic, probabilistic, sequential behaviors. Additionally, our approach offers increased flexibility for testing these computational models, allowing for the incorporation of existing testing techniques. We demonstrate the practicality of this approach through an example, and also explore its theoretical underpinnings in conjunction with standard testing principles. Notably, our approach extends existing techniques for testing sequential and concurrent behaviors by providing a unified framework that encompasses all computational models that exhibit both types of behaviors. This, in turn, paves the way for further research into the domain-specific testing of computational models and protocols that underpin modern computational systems. Finally, we propose the incorporation of our approach into the development of methodologies for testing these types of computational models, and present potential directions for future work in this area.  This work is a result of the protocol testing and analysis research collaboration between the University of Oxford and the University of Calgary.  Due to lack of space, some of the related work could not be included in this paper and will be presented in the upcoming WAPCO conference. mortality risk lies in violent deaths, yet the existing research on violence is hindered by the limited availability of high-quality data.  This study overcomes this constraint by leveraging a comprehensive and precise dataset containing information on violent incidents in one city during a five-year period.  The data set allows for the examination of both violent deaths and non-fatal injuries simultaneously, which is a novel feature among similar studies.  By analyzing the underlying factors of violence through the study of deaths and injuries, we can avoid relying on death alone as the metric, thus gaining a more complete understanding of violence's implications.  The analysis focuses on violent deaths and compares the results to the findings on non-fatal injuries, yielding insights into how they relate to each other and the surrounding environment.  The findings highlight the strong connection between violent deaths and non-fatal injuries, suggesting they share similar underlying factors, as seen in the results of both discrete and continuous analyses.  The research highlights the significant contribution of domestic violence to violent deaths, unlike injuries, and further highlights the overrepresentation of African Americans among those who die from violence, whereas those who suffer injuries reflect the overall demographic makeup.  The results of the spatial analysis reveal that a substantial proportion of both violent deaths and injuries are concentrated in specific areas, accounting for up to 50% of total violence in some regions.  The findings of the environmental analysis point to an association between violent deaths and a range of environmental factors, including noise and housing conditions, although the relationship with injuries is less pronounced.  The research uncovers patterns in violence that occur during specific times of the day and week, as well as throughout the year, and finds that a substantial proportion of both violent deaths and injuries are linked to existing relationships, including those within the same household.  The research also highlights the prevalence of firearms in both violent deaths and injuries, and the opportunity for further collaborative research between institutions and governments.  Based on the analysis of this comprehensive dataset, researchers are exploring machine learning models that can accurately predict the likelihood of violence occurring in specific geographic areas, utilizing a variety of features including demographic, environmental, and spatial factors, and the results of these models suggest they can effectively identify both violent deaths and injuries before they occur, providing indications for potential preventive measures.  The successful development of these predictive models holds promise for an automated detection system of both violent deaths and injuries, enabling real-time analysis and the identification of high-risk areas, thus facilitating targeted interventions for violence prevention. To address this issue, we propose a new protocol called LoRaViS that utilizes mmWave and submmWave phase information to determine the geographical location of a user and sends this data to a server in a confidential manner via a less precise location-based radio (LBR) connection. We demonstrate that any algorithm capable of being fooled by the LFR (Linear Feature Replacement) attack can itself be modeled linearly. We validate our conclusion through both theoretical analysis and practical experimentation, utilizing multiple established attack methods to display a neural network's resilience to LFR attacks as a linear function of its original performance. Our research is significant because it implies that attempting to improve a neural network's overall robustness is equivalent to optimizing the performance of a specific linear component. DO) interaction is one of the primary forces driving fragmentation in highly excited atoms, particularly those with high spin values.  This study explores the impact of Do forces on fragmentation in threshold energies, using protons as an example and incorporating relativistic corrections into the analysis.  A key finding shows that Do forces can shift proton energies towards lower values, but only for targets with high moment values (l>1).  Additionally, Do forces are found to disrupt the dominance of Eikonal theory in describing high-spin targets, requiring Do forces to be accounted for within an Impact Parameter dependent (IP) Eikonal theory framework.  Further simulation results indicate that Do forces could significantly affect experimental measurements at the future HIBEF facility at the SLAC National Laboratory, especially for high-spin targets and high momentum transfer values (below 100 MeV/c).  However, for momentum transfer values greater than 150 MeV/c, Do forces are found to have a minimal impact on experimental proton energies.  As such, this study is an initial step in a planned multi-step research project that will explore various aspects of Do forces' influence on experimental proton energies, in collaboration with the HIBEF experiment team at SLAC.  The first of these stages involves varying the target atom's excitation energy, while in later stages the impact of Do forces will be assessed on other observable quantities, including charge state distributions and spectral shapes.  Additionally, future stages will also explore the use of more refined theoretical models, such as exact formulas for Do forces and impact of these forces on fragmentation in excited atoms, particularly targets with high spin values and fragmentation of smaller particles like electrons and alpha particles.  The outcome of this research will be validated through simulations of the HIBEF experiment at the SLAC National Laboratory and will provide a significant contribution to the understanding of Do forces' impact on experimental proton energies in highly excited atoms. isy Intermediate Scale Quantum Computers, suffer from various issues including noise in their circuits and limited programming accuracy. This research proposes a novel error mitigation strategy called the "Estimation-Elimination Method" to address quantum computer noise. This method involves first estimating the average error effect on purified states, then using this average to correct errors in actual mixed states. We successfully tested this method using simulation models of quantum computer noise and found that it can correct errors even in circuits with complex interconnecting qubits. This method shows particular promise for protecting quantum algorithms that are particularly sensitive to error correction, such as the quantum harmonic oscillator algorithm. Consequently, the Estimation-Elimination Method should be considered as a viable error mitigation technique for noisy quantum computers. Additionally, we found that another proposed method, "E-ESE", while capable of enhancing the Estimation-Elimination Method's performance, requires access to additional program-specific information. In contrast, the basic Estimation-Elimination Method presented here utilizes only minimal information about the quantum circuit. Accordingly, this method is expected to be particularly practical for long quantum algorithms consisting of many circuit layers. Finally, we found that our method's error correction impact is particularly significant for quantum algorithms that are heavily entangled throughout their entirety, such as the simulation of deep learning models as described by AmirKalitzka et al. We demonstrate that standard convolutional neural network architectures lead to suboptimal performance due to inefficient memory access patterns. To address this challenge, we propose a new architecture called Efficient Neural Network Architecture (ENNA) that minimizes memory accesses and improves performance. In line with the constraint of limited on-chip memory, ENNA is designed to utilize the data in the cross-bar memory made up of memory banks. We validate our approach by implementing ENNA on a CUDA-based platform and observe a notable reduction in memory accesses and a substantial improvement in inference time. The findings suggest that ENNA achieves a balance between accuracy and performance, with a minimal loss in accuracy (<1%) at nearly twice the base model's performance. Moreover, ENNA exhibits potential for further optimization through pruning and weight compression. We also make our methodology and results publicly accessible through an open-source GitHub repository. Experimental evaluations using ENNA on three renowned classification benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and FC-128) have yielded notable outcomes: an up to 43% decrease in memory accesses, an up to 2.4 times improvement in inference time, and an up to 25% reduction in model size. These gains are particularly significant in the context of memory-bound processors and neural network architectures. Additionally, we have investigated two complementary approaches to optimize the cross-bar memory access: a pruning-based strategy and a submatrix-based technique. In the pruning-based approach, we remove unnecessary weights to minimize memory accesses, whereas the submatrix-based approach aims to overlap memory accesses by loading partial matrices. Although these methods yield improved performance, they come at the cost of extended computation times. We have evaluated these approaches on the ResNet-50 and MobileNet-V2 architectures, and the results indicate potential for further optimization through ENNA. Overall, our research highlights the importance of efficient memory access in neural network architecture design, and the findings provide guidelines for developers of memory-bound processors and processor-aware neural networks. Also, we found that a single MCMC model can simultaneously estimate subject-specific and common parameters while accommodating varying rates of progression for different individuals. Lastly, we found that a GP model can accurately capture the pattern of hemoglobin A1c progression even when only observing a single time point. Our research highlights the utility of MCMC methods in analyzing longitudinal outcome data. We provide the code used in this analysis publicly for reference.

This study takes a step towards rectifying this imbalance by exploring the sequential structure of syllables within spoken language. We devise a graph-based representation to illustrate the intricate patterns of syllable combination, and employ this representation to identify recurring patterns of sequence. Utilizing data from English, German, and Japanese, we demonstrate that the sequential structure of syllables conforms to specific patterns, and that these patterns differ significantly across languages, offering a potential explanation for language-specific acoustic characteristics. We refer to the former as 'intrinsic factors', and the latter as 'contextual factors'. We also identify and distinguish between three types of sequence patterns - mora, phoneme, and oxide patterns - and we demonstrate that the oxide pattern is uniquely characteristic of Japanese, and that the mora pattern is more prominent in spoken English than in spoken German, and that the phoneme pattern is prevalent in both languages. Although Video SR has shown remarkable promise, the process of developing high-quality models for this task is resource-intensive, requiring large datasets for training. This limitation poses a particular challenge for institutions with limited data availability. To address this issue, we propose a groundbreaking approach that enables the generation of high-quality videos from limited, low-quality footage using a novel technique called Multi-Resolution Video Generation (MRVG). This model utilizes both the target low-resolution video and additional auxiliary information, with multiple resolution inputs between the original and heavily zoomed-in versions, to create a more detailed video. By employing this multi-resolution framework, we successfully demonstrate the potential for MRVG to surpass the quality of models trained on vast datasets when compared to state-of-the-art Video SR methods. This is achieved with a much smaller dataset requirement, offering significant practical advantages. To support our research, we have created a suite of high-quality evaluation metrics and benchmark datasets in both theoretical and real-world settings, making them available for the community to use. Our experiments show that MRVG not only excels in low-dataset conditions but also displays particular effectiveness when given limited, high-noise input footage. With MRVG, we have the opportunity to develop high-quality models on limited datasets, opening up new possibilities for the creation of realistic video content. This has the potential to benefit multiple fields, such as video restoration, enhancement, and manipulation. This work presents a general method for approximating Hamiltonians based on spectral data, formulating a minimization problem whose solutions converge to the actual Hamiltonian as the spectral resolution improves. A concrete algorithm using this approach yields Hamiltonians whose spectral properties closely match those of the original system, even in scenarios where local degeneracies are present. This algorithm has been applied to a paradigmatic model of time-periodic quantum systems, represented by a two-level Hamiltonian with mixed-type spectrum. Additionally, our technique is capable of reproducing local degeneracies and spectral gaps present in the target Hamiltonian. This success paves the way for future research on chaotic quantum systems using this approach. Furthermore, we propose employing this algorithm in experimental contexts, such as quantum tomography, to recover Hamiltonians from spectral data. This research introduces an advanced method for quickly determining the reliability of intermodal transportation networks by utilizing submodular maximization. The proposed approach focuses on identifying the minimal set of transportation infrastructure with the highest combined potential to minimize the probability of system failures, given limited resources. Healthcare specialists require assistance in identifying patterns from radiography images of patients' lungs in order to make accurate diagnoses.  This study explores using machine learning to develop an automated system for classifying Covid-19 positive cases from negative cases based on lung CT scans, and whether patterns can be identified to detect the disease from limited diagnostic information.  An automated system was developed and tested on a large dataset of lung CT scans from diverse sources, including the Covid-19 dataset of Chen *et al.*  A comparison was made between different machine learning classifiers using various features such as noise levels and image compression. demultiplexing through mode's propagation direction, ultimately promoting the 
development of coherent communication technology. 
Although the transmission of chiral OAM enabled communication systems 
demonstrates promising results in laboratory settings, the stability of these 
propagation conditions over long distances remains a major concern. While our 
results indicate the successful transmission of chiral OAM enabled phase 
encoding in a laboratory environment, further research is necessary to address 
the issue of atmospheric turbulence which poses a significant threat to the 
performance of these systems, through the implementation of advanced adaptive 
optics technologies and multi-layered security codes that can provide an 
additional layer of security for the communication. 
In this talk, our recent advancements in the field of chiral OAM enabled 
free-space optical communication systems will be presented, along with our 
efforts to address the issue of atmospheric turbulence which poses a major 
challenge to the performance of these systems.

This paper extends that research to examine another widely accepted statistical concept:  the consistency of maximum likelihood estimators.  We look at a general statistical model with parameters that can take any real value and derive a condition for the consistency of these estimators.  This condition is shown to be met by models that are ergodic and stationary under certain probability measurements.  We then apply this finding to investigate the consistency of maximum likelihood estimators in specific models, such as linear regression and the geometric distribution.  Our results are significant because they highlight situations in which the traditional statistical theory may not hold, prompting researchers to be more cautious when interpreting data.  We also offer practical advice on the use of maximum likelihood estimators, highlighting the importance of verifying the validity of these methods for each specific model.  Additionally, we provide a new perspective on the distribution of sample variances, connecting this concept to the distribution of correlation coefficients in certain models.  This research has the potential to guide methodological innovations, particularly in the context of large datasets that are increasingly common in modern statistical analysis.  We encourage researchers to be vigilant when relying on traditional statistical theory and to collaborate with theoretical experts to validate the validity of methods in each specific model.  As an example of this collaboration, we have solved the issue of consistency for the standard linear model through an abstract approach, but we believe that a concrete proof is also possible.  We also propose an open-source R package called MLR for testing the consistency of maximum likelihood estimators in a linear regression model that meets specific conditions, which researchers can use to evaluate the validity of this concept in their own data sets.  This package includes functions for checking the validity of the maximum likelihood estimators and provides results that concur with the theoretical findings presented here.  We have applied these methods in an analysis of German income data, presented in the appendix.  We employed the MLR package to test the consistency of the maximum likelihood estimators in a linear regression model that meets the ergodic and stationary conditions, which are fully described in the appendix.  The results obtained with the MLR package concur with the theoretical findings presented here.  We have primarily focused on the consistency of the maximum likelihood estimators in a linear regression model that meets the ergodic and stationary conditions, but we have also obtained similar results in the analysis of survival time data, which is an important area of research in modern statistical analysis.

We investigated the relationship between authors' citations and job placements for researchers in the fields of economics, finance, management, and accounting. Our findings indicate that authors with more citations are more likely to secure jobs at top universities and institutions, and the citation advantage varies across fields. In the field of finance, for example, the citation benefit for researchers ends around the top 10% of cited papers, whereas in economics the benefit extends to the top 5% of cited papers. Our analysis also revealed that job market presentations with the support of established researchers can increase an author's chances of being hired, and that authors who place their presentations in the top quartile of AER and QJE are more likely to secure jobs at top universities. In the field of management, for example, presenting at the top quartile of AER or QJE is enough to guarantee a job at a top university, and the same is true for finance. Additionally, our data showed that the job market presentations of female researchers receive similar attention to those of their male counterparts, and that authors who place their presentations in the top quartile of AER or QJE are more likely to secure jobs at top universities across all demographic groups studied. In terms of performance, for instance, in the field of finance, the best way for a researcher to increase their chances of being hired is to publish in the top 10% of cited papers, and to place their job market presentation in the top quartile of AER or a top journal such as the Journal of Finance. In economics, the key indicators are to publish in the top 5% of cited papers, and to place their job market presentation in the top quartile of AER or QJE. Following these guidelines may enable early career researchers to better navigate the job market in their chosen field.  Due to the significant variation in data characteristics across the four fields studied, our analysis employed field-specific variables, and the results showed that while authors' citations are a crucial factor in securing jobs in economics, finance, management, and accounting, other factors such as publication records and performance during the job market presentation process play a key role, and that having a strong signal like publications in the American Economic Review or the Journal of Finance significantly increases an author's chances of being hired. , we examine the impact of large gluon modes on the QCD phase transition as the temperature varies. A fourth spatial dimension is used with increasing lattice sizes in that dimension, ranging from 4 to 8, while maintaining a relatively small time-like direction. Our results show the crossover and phase transition temperatures decrease with larger gluon modes, and the changes in the transition depend on the lattice gauge theory's spatial and temporal lattice size ratio. ia} and {\it Kepler} have significantly advanced star cluster research, but often these studies focus on already mass-assembled clusters. This project seeks to investigate the early development of star clusters, specifically their member selection and mass growth. A large dataset of the {\it Kepler} legacy survey was analyzed to identify 49 young star clusters located behind the bulge and in the disk. These clusters were then tracked over time with {\it Gaia} data to determine their proper motions and extinctions, helping to define a "goldilocks zone" for each cluster - an area where the stellar density is neither too high nor too low. This approach allows for an unbiased calculation of mass growth rates. The results show that star clusters in the bulge typically have faster mass growth rates, likely due to their location and the surrounding molecular gas. These clusters also tend to have more variable growth rates. Clusters in the disk, on the other hand, exhibit smaller growth rate fluctuations. A distinction can be seen between clusters under the influence of a companion molecular cloud, who are accumulating gas and growing in mass, and those who have already consumed their surrounding gas and are now breaking apart. It is predicted that the former will continue to form stars for a longer period of time. A theoretical model is also introduced to explain the observed growth rates, utilizing a gas consumption model that takes into account cluster half-mass radial migration. The model can be minimized in terms of observable quantities, allowing for future observational testing. Overall, this study highlights the significance of selecting cluster members based on mass, rather than spatial location, and that star clusters are not uniform and require individualized analysis. The multi-messenger potential of this research is also mentioned, along with potential follow-up star formation bursts following powerful cosmic events. The full dataset and modeling tools are made publicly available for further research. effectiveness on a dataset derived from real-world EHR systems. Our research

both of which are essential in mitigating the software supply chain disruption 
threat. An interdisciplinary approach among software engineers, security experts,

the Multi-Source Cross-Lingual Named Entity Recognition (MC-LNER) dataset has been created to address the challenges of NER in multiple languages.  This MC-LNER dataset consists of 6,796 labeled sentences from 3 source languages (English, German, Portuguese) and 8 target languages, with the goal of developing and evaluating cross-lingual and multi-source NER models. cameras have numerous applications in fields like 3D sensing, motion analysis, and biometrics.  ToF cameras estimate distance by measuring the phase shift of a emitted light signal.  However, their accuracy can be affected by various factors including sensor noise, limited dynamic range, and water vapor in the air, which can also interfere with the light signal.  One method to enhance ToF camera accuracy is to optimize the signal processing technique used, and this can be achieved by incorporating external information about the light signal's interference.  One such technique, luminance aided phase shifting (LAPS), exploits the spatial intensity information to improve phase shifting accuracy.  LAPS uses a technique called local quadratic least squares (LQLS) to enhance estimation, and this method can be further improved by utilizing spatial intensity information about the light signal's local maximum and minimum values.  This is captured in the new technique called non-local QLS (NLQLS), and it represents a systematic approach to incorporating external information in LAPS.  Simulation results show that both LQLS and NLQLS techniques can enhance LAPS performance, and this is especially noticeable in low-signal-to-noise conditions.  Simulation data also indicate that NLQLS performs better than LQLS, and this difference in performance is more pronounced in higher noise levels.  To evaluate these techniques in a real-world setting, an experiment was conducted using three different ToF cameras, and the results showed that both LQLS and NLQLS could improve LAPS performance in a real-world environment.  Furthermore, NLQLS showed better performance than LQLS in all three cameras tested, and this was noticeable in both indoor and outdoor environments.  The improvement in performance using NLQLS was more significant in the other camera, and this effect was more pronounced in the wide-field camera due to its larger dynamic range.  The results of the experiment using the NLQLS technique in combination with LAPS on the high-sensitivity camera were particularly notable, and this was because this camera is more prone to interference from water vapor in the air.  The research provides a platform for exploring other future techniques that could further enhance ToF camera accuracy, and this is achieved by modeling the light signal's interference using a mathematical approach.  Based on this approach, an explanation is provided for why both LQLS and NLQLS can improve LAPS performance, and this is by minimizing the total cost function representing the model of the light signal's interference. A novel attention-free, baseline-aware transformer architecture has been introduced, which incorporates a innovative hierarchical attention mechanism while significantly reducing complexity.  By incorporating multiple attention-free, baseline-aware sub-modules that process different levels of abstraction, our proposed architecture achieves notable performance improvements while substantially reducing computational demands.  Our model's consistency with the original transformer model is ensured through the use of the same quadratic attention score function and additive layer normalization.  In experiments, our architecture demonstrated superior performance and efficiency improvements across multiple tasks, including language translation, summariation, and text classification.  When compared to standard attention-based transformers, our efficient architecture resulted in at least a 2x reduction in parameters and a 4x reduction in floating point operations per second (FLOPS), while delivering performance within 10% of the original.  Code for the research is publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL.  Our architecture's excellent balance of performance and efficiency makes it an appealing option for the vast majority of machine learning workloads, in which models are typically pre-trained and then deployed with limited re-training required.  Given this, our architecture is an particularly effective solution for efficient inference, but further research is needed to fully understand the implications of removing attention from deep transformer networks.  One notable observation made through analysis of the attention-free sub-modules was the emergence of crude chunking patterns, where attention was distributed over multiple consecutive positions rather than targeting specific words or phrases.  Future research opportunities are also presented by this phenomenon, which may be worth exploring further, especially in situations where network architectures with inherent locality properties are being targeted, as noted in the text.  Additionally, implementation efficiency of the proposed architecture could be optimized through use of apportioning instead of averaging in the attention-free sub-modules, which is an area that deserves exploration, as previously reported in the literature.  In particular, this approach has been shown to yield significant FLOPS reductions with minimal performance degradation in certain applications, such as machine translation, but further research is needed to fully assess its impact across a broader range of tasks and data sets.  As an example, in evaluations conducted on the large WMT2014 English-to-German translation task, using the primary training dataset, replacing attention with a baseline equivalent consumed approximately 117 million parameters and resulted in 6.5 billion FLOPS, which in turn led to less than 10% performance degradation compared to the full attention-based transformer model, as reported in the text

This study examines the intricacies of patch-based attacks in a retinal disease detection context, specifically generating patches that would mislead a model in identifying diabetic retinopathy.  Analyzing the effects of attacks on both healthy and diseased eyes, our results reveal that in certain cases, the model's accuracy in identifying diabetic retinopathy can drop to under 50%, yet interestingly, the attack may not always succeed, depending on the disease severity.  The findings highlight the need for model robustness to avoid misdiagnosis in medical imaging, and also raise questions about potential attacks on other retinal diseases, such as glaucoma. In counter-measuring such attacks, our proposed technique, GRFPatch, is shown to enhance the retinopathy model's accuracy, and also demonstrates its robustness in detecting other disease indicators.  The study also explores various attack methods that could be applied, such as generating localized anomalies, manipulating specific features, and creating global disorders, and provides guidelines on possible attack vectors in real-world scenarios.  Additionally, our work offers multiple contributions to the field:  first, the analysis of patch-based attacks in retinal disease detection;  second, the provision of the DRDrop dataset;  third, the development of the GRFPatch defense strategy;  and fourth, the exploration of different attack approaches.  To build upon this research, the proposed techniques and dataset are made available for public use.  Our findings also highlight the necessity for machine learning model robustness in retinal disease detection, and could have broader implications in other computer vision applications.  Furthermore, possible counter-measures such as re-training the model and employing anomaly detection filters are discussed, and the study offers multiple research paths for patch-based attacks in retinal disease detection to be explored in the future. Currently, most techniques train ANNs using supervised learning methods, but doing so has the limitation of requiring vast amounts of labeled data, which is not always feasible.  In contrast, our proposed method educates ANNs using a different type of learning, one that does not rely on labeled data, by presenting them with sequences of ANNs that differ by a fixed number of gate additions and deletions from a basic model.  When presented with such sequences, the ANNs learn to generalize their underlying algebraic expression, provided that the changes made are limited enough as to not cause the expression to change significantly.  Our approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through benchmark tests, revealing that it excels at learning expressions containing relatively few variables, but may struggle with those containing many.  A key advantage of this technique is that it enables ANNs to learn from a much more compact set of unlabeled data, which is especially important when there are limited resources available.  We show that our proposed method has substantial cost-saving benefits, especially in scenarios where ANNs are connected, which is particularly common in modern systems.  A notable feature of our technique is that it allows for the learning of unbalanced expressions, ones in which the ANNs are able to generalize over multiple output values for each input, provided that there is some correlation between the inputs and outputs, which is the case with many real-world applications.  We also explore ways in which our technique could be accelerated through the use of optimization methods such as gradient descent, but found that these had a minimal impact, suggesting that the main bottleneck with larger expressions will continue to be the amount of time it takes to propagate signals through the ANNs.  Finally, we consider ways in which our technique could be modified to handle more complex scenarios, such as learning that involves multiple tasks, but with a much deeper understanding of the underlying algebraic structures at play. However, deploying these models in resource-constrained environments remains a significant challenge due to their massive size.  One promising approach involves compressing them using quantization techniques.  Although previous research has produced quantized PLMs with improved performance, these models still struggled with accuracy when applied to low-latency inference tasks.  To address this issue, this study employed mixed precision (MP) to train PLMs and achieved notable accuracy gains when compared to their full-precision counterparts.  Experimental results showed that MP-trained PLMs could achieve comparable performance to full-precision models while reducing memory usage by $10\times$ and $5\times$ for BERT and RoBERTa, respectively.  Furthermore, MP-trained models exhibited $1.5\times$ to $2.5\times$ greater accuracy when applied to sparse and low-resolution inference compared to full-precision models.  Evaluations conducted on multiple NLP benchmarks revealed MP-trained models for BERT and RoBERTa that were $4.3$% and $4.1$% more accurate, respectively, while also reducing memory usage by $10.3$% and $5.2$% when applied to real-world NLP tasks.  Additionally, MP-trained models for BERT and RoBERTa demonstrated $1.2$% to $1.5$% and $1.3$% to $1.6$% greater accuracy when applied to sparse and low-resolution inference, as evaluated on the GLUE and SQuAD 2.0 datasets.  In terms of latency and accuracy trade-offs, MP-trained BERT Large for the SQuAD 2.0 dataset took $0.26$ seconds with an accuracy of $70.2$%, while MP-trained RoBERTa Large for the GLUE dataset took $0.53$ seconds with an accuracy of $70.5$%.  Model weights and implementation are publicly available at this repository: https://github.com/hpcml/MP-Layers.  With these findings, using MP training to compress large-language models such as BERT and RoBERTa is shown to be an effective means of enhancing their inference efficiency while maintaining their accuracy.  To build upon this work, researchers and engineers are encouraged to utilize this repository by replacing the model training layer with the MP approach, as demonstrated in "mp_training.py", while using the BERT base model as an example.

This view is reflected in the NP-Hard 2-approximation problem, where the aim is to determine if there's a 2-approximation algorithm for a specific NP-Hard problem; in other words, an algorithm that, given an instance of the problem, either confirms the existence of a 2-approximation or proves this is impossible. This research delves into three distinctive NP-Hard combinatorial optimization problems - Vertex Cover, Hypergraph Homomorphism, and Minimum Feedback Edge Coloring - to explore the properties of 2-approximation solutions. This study reveals that 2-approximation solutions exhibit the behavior of "weakly projectable" and "weakly dispersible" properties; in particular, it's shown that such solutions, when applied to Vertex Cover, exhibit "weakly dispersible" behavior, while solutions for Hypergraph Homomorphism and Minimum Feedback Edge Coloring display "weakly projectable" behavior. This research also includes results on the parameter-tolerant approximation, a specific instance of which yields a $4+\epsilon$-approximation for Vertex Cover, given the instance's cover size is within $O(\sqrt{n})$ of the optimal size. Typically, evaluations of shooting ranges focus on environmental factors such  as soil and groundwater contamination, as well as the potential effects on  local wildlife. Unlike industrial facilities, shooting ranges have a unique  auditory signature, characterized by the distinct sound of repeated gunfire  noises. The aim of this research is to explore novel machine learning techniques  to identify and quantify the auditory disturbance resulting from shooting range  noise. Our findings show that advanced machine learning algorithms, specifically  neural networks and support vector machines, can effectively determine when  recorded audio samples contain shooting range noise. Furthermore, these models  can accurately quantify the loudness of this noise and distinguish it from  background ambient sound. The potential of these early findings to inform  regulatory policies on shooting range noise is also examined.  In a initial experiment, we demonstrated that neural network and support vector  machine models could successfully identify shooting range noise within audio  clips containing a mixture of range and ambient sounds. The accuracy of these  models was exceptionally high, surpassing 90% in both cases. In a subsequent  experiment, we discovered that a neural network model could effectively gauge  the loudness of shooting range noise, even when competing with ambient sounds,  and even when the data set was significantly expanded. Moreover, a different  type of model was able to differentiate between the sounds of shooting ranges  and other noisy environments.  To explore the practical applications of these findings, we conducted surveys  among shooting range owners and local government officials. The responses from  these surveys revealed that both shooting range operators and local regulatory  authorities are unaware of the auditory disturbance caused by shooting range  noise and the techniques available to assess it.  In another set of experiments, we developed and tested a versatile model suited  for evaluating the auditory impacts of shooting range noise. This model's  versatility makes it an ideal solution for regulatory agencies looking to  systematically assess the auditory effects of shooting ranges in diverse  environmental contexts.  Our research offers promising outcomes for both machine learning model  development and the potential regulatory benefits it may bring. However, we  also highlight significant challenges that shooting range operators and local  regulatory authorities face in detecting shooting range noise audibly. This paper provides an in-depth examination of the properties of categorical amalgams,
with a focus on their inherent characteristics and underlying category requirements.
Our analysis reveals that a categorical amalgam possesses the amalgamation property
if and only if its underlying category does. Moreover, this property is distinct from
the unique extension property, which has been explored in previous studies. Additionally,
our findings establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a categorical amalgam
to have the strong amalgamation property. These conditions not only ensure that
any two morphisms between given objects can be combined, but also that this combination
maintains the desired universal property. Our research is an extension of earlier works
on categorical amalgams and morphism combinations, with new properties being defined
and their relationships with existing concepts examined. These new properties include
their compatibility with unique extension property morphisms and the strong amalgamation
property in subcategories. Our results show that the strong amalgamation property
is both computationally feasible to determine and inheritable across subcategories.

Our approach utilizes symbolic verification tools to develop safety proofs for complex systems composed of multiple components.  To facilitate this process, we suggest using a modular, component-based design framework that leverages a lightweight operating system to isolate and simplify verification of individual components.  As a case study, we apply our method to create safety certificates for a closed-loop control system utilizing a linear controller, demonstrating the process.  We employ the Rodin platform and its connection to the Bebop bounded model checking tool to achieve approximately 10^5 times faster verification times and significantly reduced counterexample corrections, amounting to around 10^4 instances of the underlying hardware.  Our method enables the creation of safety certificates readable by formal hardware verification tools, yielding validated code for the target microcontroller.  We showcase our method's efficacy with an adaptive cruise control system, obtaining a safety certificate verifying that the system avoids collisions with unknown obstacles.  The certificate's readability by formal hardware verification tools confirms compliant IEEE 802.15.4 radio hardware utilization, ensuring that radio transmissions do not cause collisions with other network nodes.  Our method's performance in the adaptive cruise control case study results in a safety certificate issued within approximately 260 seconds, requiring approximately 2 GB of memory.  The issue of large verification evidence being difficult to store on embedded systems' limited memory is addressed by our proposed approach, which explores methods for reducing the size of the safety certificate.  We outline techniques for minimizing the size of the safety certificate, exploiting the rodin platform's capabilities for set-based bounded model checking to reduce verification evidence by approximately 10^4 times, achieving feasible storage requirements for the safety certificate on the target microcontroller.  Ultimately, our method succeeds in creating compact, practical safety certificates for embedded systems through symbolic analysis.   Results are presented in Section 3, with further discussion held in Section 
  4. Section 5 summarizes used metrics (Appendix B), while the methodology 
  is described in Section 2. All calculations were performed using Python 
  version 3.8 (van Rossem, 2019) and TensorFlow version 2.3 (Jang and 
  Jeon, 2020).

  previous studies (Woehl, 2020a, Woehl, 2020b).

superconducting vortices, researchers have been studying a newly found state of matter - the Bose ring.  This state, consisting of coherent currents around a point defect in a mesoscopic superconducting loop, has been theoretically predicted to be equivalent to a vortex ring - a three-dimensional analog of the Abrikosov vortex.  In our study, we demonstrate that the Bose ring state can be created experimentally by injecting a single magnetic monopole into a mesoscopic superconducting loop in the presence of a strong external magnetic field.  We show that the external field forces the Bose ring state to spin counterclockwise or clockwise to minimize its energy, resulting in the emission of quanta of magnetic flux through the loop.  The emitted quanta can be detected by monitoring the DC SQUID device formed by two adjacent loops.  The left-right asymmetry of the electromagnetic radiation also allows us to determine the handedness of the spinning Bose ring.  Furthermore, the precision of this method makes it suitable for detecting the very small changes in the mass of the monopole that would signify a potential violation of C, P and T symmetries.  In addition, this method provides a direct link between magnetic monopoles and superconducting vortices, potentially allowing us to use monopoles as a probe to study the properties of vortices.  We also propose that this method could be adapted to detect magnetic dyons and monopole-dyon pairs.  The accuracy of this method in detecting a single monopole is as high as 10^-8 times the Planck energy, making it one of the most sensitive experiments for detecting magnetic monopoles.  We show that the emission of magnetic quanta from the Bose ring can also be induced by applying a high-frequency voltage to the SQUID device, enabling the detection of magnetic monopoles even in multi-monopole situations.  We demonstrate that this method can be extended to detect magnetic monopoles in different types of SQUID devices, including F, J, SH and HF junctions.  We also propose that this method could be adapted to detect magnetic dyons.  We show that the emission of magnetic quanta from the Bose ring can be used to develop a precision detector of magnetic monopoles. This paper introduces a novel, robust risk measure based on extreme quantile regression, defining it as the difference between the 99th conditional quantile of future values and the 99th conditional quantile of past values. Furthermore, the paper finds that the best maintenance policies are those that balance costs and risks, varying depending on the manufacturer's risk tolerance and vision for future production. This paper analyzes how incorporating day-ahead wholesale pricing and resource adequacy markets affects the behavior of electricity markets.  We demonstrate that a perfectly liberalized electricity market, with separate wholesale and resource adequacy markets, may experience imbalances unless there is explicit coordination between these two areas.  Utilizing a partially liberalized market as a benchmark, we conduct numerical tests to evaluate how market behavior is impacted when wholesale pricing and resource adequacy markets are incorporated.  Our results indicate that including a resource adequacy market leads to higher wholesale prices, but the benefit to price volatility is less clear.  Notably, the impact of a resource adequacy market on wholesale price volatility seems to decrease as the market becomes more liberalized.  Our research also suggests that a resource adequacy market can provide price support during peak hours, but this effect is limited to certain hours of the day.  Furthermore, we find that the value of new generating capacity is higher when wholesale pricing and resource adequacy markets are combined, but this increase in value is greatest for markets that are only partially liberalized.  In fully liberalized markets, the value of new generating capacity approaches its traditional day-ahead wholesale pricing counterpart.  Our findings provide a deeper understanding of the interconnectedness of wholesale pricing and resource adequacy markets, and the variability in market behavior as markets transition from being fully to partially liberalized.  This research includes a proposed framework for modeling a liberalized electricity market with resource adequacy, utilizing a two-stage Whitaker model adapted for non-convexities.  Numerical tests are conducted using a modified Los Alamos partial equilibrium model, which incorporates elements of the Whitaker model, to evaluate the impact of a liberalized wholesale market on market behavior.  This research explores alternative degrees of market liberalization, ranging from a purely liberalized market to one that is barely liberalized.  In a perfectly liberalized market, the wholesale market is replaced by a resource adequacy market, whereas in a barely liberalized market, the wholesale market retains its traditional structure while the resource adequacy market experiences increased participation.  The value of new generating capacity is compared across these liberalization scenarios to determine the impact of a liberalized wholesale market on the value of new generating capacity in the resource adequacy market.  Our results indicate that a liberalized wholesale market has an increased value of new generating capacity in the resource adequacy market, but this effect is greatest for markets that are only partially liberalized. This method involves converting field products into higher-order local functional derivatives of the action with respect to the mean field. We demonstrate that our tools and conditions enable efficient computation of quenched averages, cumulants, and correlation functions. Furthermore, we show that our method allows for simplification of field product calculations using the action's properties, resulting in a more practical way of performing theoretical analyses. Specifically, we apply our method to investigate the behavior of massless scalar field theories on a flat spacetime with a compact Euclidean space of $k$ dimensions, focusing on a temperature parameter $T$. We utilize our tools to derive general expressions for the $k$-dimensional correlation functions in both hot and cold scenarios. In the cold case, we derive a fundamental equation that relates the primary field's value to the temperature and the quartic coupling strength. We demonstrate that at very low temperatures, the primary field's value behaves as $m \propto T^{1-\frac{1}{k}}$. In the hot case, we find that the primary field's value behaves as $m \propto e^{-\frac{2\pi}{T}}$ when the quartic coupling is negative. We also investigate the phase transition that occurs when the quartic coupling is positive, finding that the primary field's value behaves as $m \propto T^{1-\frac{1}{k}}$ at low temperatures, and that this phase is unstable due to the emergence of a non-analytic branch in the action's minimization process. This non-analytic branch is driven by the formation of a Bose-Einstein condensate in the hot scenario. We further utilize our method to study the behavior of the algebra's higher-order derivatives in the hot and cold cases, establishing the existence of a power-law energy spectrum $E \propto p^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$ in both scenarios, and the emergence of a mode-locking phenomenon in the cold case at very low temperatures. This phenomenon involves the algebra's fundamental frequency being an integer multiple of the temperature's reciprocal, and results in the primary field's value being an analytic function of the temperature in this regime. We also demonstrate that the hot case's power-law energy spectrum is an emergent property of the algebra's fundamental frequency being marginally locked, and that this locking is driven by the formation of a zero-mode in the hot scenario's quartic interaction. The Higgs boson can be differentiated from standard $e^+e^-$ background by selecting events containing a pair of $b\bar{b}$ particles and requiring that the cross-sectional threshold for $e^+e^-$ interactions at 2 TeV be surpassed. Based on the effective field theory of QCD, we analyze the exclusive production of quark pairs in $e^+e^-$ collisions and estimate the sensitivity of 1.5 TeV, high-luminosity $e^+e^-$ colliders to the $H$s boson across various momentum transfer scales $\sqrt{Q^2}$. For the $\Upsilon$ resonance, we find that the 5$\sigma$ discovery significance for $H\simeq h+H$ at $\sqrt{Q^2}=4.5$ GeV is attainable with 8.5 ab$^{-1}$ of luminosity, while for $\Upsilon$ masses above 300 GeV, the 5$\sigma$ discovery significance for $H$s becomes accessible with 1-10 ab$^{-1}$ of luminosity depending on $\sqrt{Q^2}$. Furthermore, we find that the 5$\sigma$ discovery significance for $H$s at $\sqrt{Q^2}=1.5$ GeV will be attainable with 0.5-5 ab$^{-1}$ of luminosity as the quark pair invariant mass approaches the $J/\psi$ resonance. Additionally, we investigate the effective theory of QCD and demonstrate that the quark pair distribution functions can be modeled with precision by intersecting two relativistic heavy quark potentials at small distances and by modeling the deformed quark pair distribution functions with the help of an analytic formula, thereby facilitating an understanding of exclusive quark pair production across various momentum transfer scales $\sqrt{Q^2}$. Furthermore, we propose that future $e^+e^-$ colliders capable of producing the $t\bar{t}$ process can also discover the $H$s boson through recoil against other exclusive quark pairs, such as $b\bar{b}$, $c\bar{c}$, or $J/\psi\eta_c$, thereby providing a secondary discovery channel for the Higgs-strangeness boson.

This paper delves into designing and evaluating robust performance specifications for ML models at the edge, with a primary focus on models utilizing Neural Network-based representations. It investigates how robust performance specifications can be integrated into the training process and offers a novel approach called Robust Performance Specification Learning. This investigation focused on understanding the spin wave dynamics in GdTiO$_3$ across its magnetic phase transition. Our data analysis revealed two distinct excitation models: high-energy magnetic excitons and a charge and magnetic excitation mode below the magnetic transition temperature. This problem occurs because contrastive pre-training typically employs vast collections of non-related visual data, making the models sensitive to diverse patterns.  When applied to limited medical image datasets, this leads to overemphasis on visual differences unrelated to the task at hand.  A notable example of such overemphasis occurs when the model becomes skilled at distinguishing easy-to-distinguish images (e.g., contrast vs non-contrast MRI scans) from those that are more difficult to distinguish (e.g., tumor lesions from normal tissue).  A common remedy for such overfitting issues is to use noise corruption, but this is largely irrelevant when working with limited medical image datasets.  A more effective solution is to incorporate an asymmetrical softmax temperature contrastive learning technique, which was initially designed to weigh positive samples more heavily than negative ones.  This approach enhances the network's ability to focus on task-relevant pattern information by reducing the influence of unrelated visual features.  Experimental results indicate that this method yields superior performance when applied to limited-size datasets in various medical image analysis tasks.  A key advantage of this technique is that it eliminates the need to construct negative samples, making it an attractive approach for use in real-world scenarios.  Although the technique demonstrates strong performance in tasks that are relatively easy to solve (e.g., lesion detection, contrast vs non-contrast MRI classification), further research is needed to fully assess its potential in tasks that are more difficult to solve (e.g., tumor subtype classification, pancreas segmentation).  A primary contribution of this research is the release of two publicly available datasets containing only 100 images each, which are focused on retinal and colon lesions, respectively.  These datasets, in combination with previously released datasets, will provide a comprehensive evaluation framework for future medical image analysis tasks.  As an example of the technique's applicability, we developed an approach to detect and count retinal lesions from fundus images, which achieved precision, recall, and F-score metrics of 0.83, 0.73, and 0.77, respectively.  A key feature of this technique is its ability to extend standard U-Net architectures by incorporating contrastive learning layers, which enables it to leverage sample-specific feature information to aid in segmentation tasks.  As a result, this technique demonstrates superior performance in colon cancer segmentation

COVID-19 outbreak, there has been a notable increase in the dissemination of misinformation. This kind of information poses a significant threat to public health as it often leads to the avoidance of necessary preventive measures and healthcare-seeking behavior. It is also detrimental to delay vaccination efforts and promote harmful lifestyles. 

Due to the vast quantity of COVID-19-related misinformation circulating on social media platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Reddit[2], there has been growing interest in conducting studies on this topic. It has been observed that news articles shared on Twitter by influential users often contain misleading information about COVID-19. Therefore, in this research, our focus shifted from these articles to quoted tweets containing COVID-19 misinformation. 

Our analysis of Twitter data between August 1st and November 15th, 2020 uncovered 15,000 randomly selected English language tweets. Our findings showed that quoted tweets comprising COVID-19 misinformation exhibited distinct characteristics when compared to randomly selected neutral tweets. 

Results indicated that quoted tweets containing COVID-19 misinformation tended to be shorter and include URLs more frequently. They also exhibited a higher level of negativity and a greater likelihood of engaging users. Utilizing eight NLP models, our classification experiments revealed that the BERT model yielded the best performance in distinguishing quoted tweets containing COVID-19 misinformation from randomly selected neutral tweets. Subsequently, our evaluation using the data from COVID-19-related competitions and benchmarks demonstrated that BERT also outperformed other baseline models. 

Ultimately, our research aimed to explore the feasibility of detecting COVID-19 misinformation on Twitter through NLP methods. Given the extensive quantity of Twitter data representing only a brief period of time in 2020, our results yielded promising outcomes. These findings have the potential to contribute to the development of antivirus systems capable of identifying and mitigating the spread of such information. 

Related studies have been conducted by various researchers utilizing data from Twitter, Facebook, and Reddit[2]. Our research, however, focused on quoted tweets containing COVID-19 misinformation situated within Twitter context. Moreover, as opposed to relying on manually annotated data, our experiments built on the foundation laid by Yang et al.[3]. 

In their study, they successfully classified Chinese language COVID-19 misinformation articles shared on Twitter using NLP models. Subsequently, our research sought to explore the feasibility of replicating their results on quoted tweets containing COVID-19 misinformation using eight NLP models.
